title: The Mevlevi
hook: Rumi's order still turns in Konya, a ceremony of remembrance, not a performance

segments.voice: Yesterday, khalwa: the Sufi retreat, a room emptied of company and given to remembrance. Your line was khalwa. Did you find your hour, or at least put it on the calendar? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-one.

A reed flute sounds a long, breathy note while everyone sits still. Then men in tall felt hats and black cloaks walk slowly around the floor and bow to one another. The cloaks are set aside, and long white robes show underneath. Their arms are crossed over their chests. One by one they unfold them, the right hand turned up, the left hand turned down, and they begin to turn. In English they're called whirling dervishes, and to anyone watching, it can look like a dance. Today is about why, in their own tradition, it's something else entirely.
screen: `A REED FLUTE, A LONG NOTE.` → `BLACK CLOAKS SET ASIDE.` → `THEY BEGIN TO TURN.`

segments.voice: The Mevlevi order traces itself to Jalal al-Din Rumi, the poet, and takes its name from the title his followers gave him: Mevlana, our master. Its ceremony is the sema, from an Arabic word for listening. That's the first surprise. The name isn't about turning. It's about hearing. Rumi's long poem, the Masnavi, opens with the instrument heard in the ceremony: a reed flute, cut from the reed bed, crying out its longing to go back where it came from. Readers of Rumi hear the reed as the human soul, homesick for its source. Tradition reads the clothing too. The tall hat is said to stand for a tombstone, the white robe for a shroud, and the black cloak set aside at the start for the grave left behind. The right hand, turned up, receives from heaven. The left, turned down, passes it on to the earth. The one turning stands in between, giving away what comes. And the whole of it is remembrance of God, dhikr. That's why the Mevlevi call it a ceremony, not a performance. The turners aren't playing to a crowd; their attention is somewhere else. Where the sema is held as worship, guests may be asked not to applaud at the end, because applause would turn a prayer into a show. In Konya, the city where Rumi is buried, the turning goes on. Tradition calls the night of his death his wedding night, the night he went home to the Beloved, and the sema keeps it. A reed's longing, and a whole ceremony built around listening for home.
screen: `SEMA MEANS LISTENING.` · `THE REED, CUT FROM ITS BED.` · `ONE HAND UP, ONE HAND DOWN.` · `A CEREMONY, NOT A PERFORMANCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, in two parts. First, now: sit the way a guest sits at a sema, still and attentive, hands resting. Listen. Not to a song, but to whatever is here: the hum of the room, your own breath, the long out-breath like a note on a reed. Let your attention go where the turners' attention goes, away from being seen. If you pray, let the listening be remembrance. If you don't, let it simply be listening. Later, if you can, watch a recording of a sema the way you'd sit in a house of prayer: quietly, to the end. The bell holds the time.
The Mevlevi. Rumi's order, whose sema, the turning ceremony, is remembrance of God and a kind of listening, not a performance. Today's word.

Your line: not a performance. Today, do one thing you'd usually do with an eye on who's watching, a kind act, a good piece of work, a gift, and let nobody see it. Let it be for its own sake. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Mevlevi dervishes perform the sema as an act of remembrance of God, turning to the music of the reed flute and drums; in Konya and elsewhere the ceremony is held on set occasions, and guests are asked to watch quietly, as at worship.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Mevlevi are dancers who spin for an audience.
what it means: Rumi's order, whose turning ceremony is remembrance of God, done as worship, not a show.
what a scholar hears: sema, listening, opening like the Masnavi with the reed flute's longing, and a tradition that reads hat, robe and hands as death, return and giving.

notes: The Masnavi's opening (the reed's lament) is paraphrased; Whinfield 1898 has an abridged translation, but its wording was not checked, so nothing is quoted.
The name Mevlevi from Mevlana ('our master'), and sema from Arabic sama' ('listening'), are stated; confirm.
Symbolism of hat (sikke, tombstone), white robe (tennure, shroud), black cloak (hirka, grave) and the hands (right up receiving, left down giving) is attributed to 'tradition'; confirm.
'Where the sema is held as worship, guests may be asked not to applaud' is kept conditional; practice varies between venues. Confirm.
Rumi's burial in Konya and the 'wedding night' (Seb-i Arus) are stated without a date under the claims rule; confirm.
The hook says 'men'; confirm whether to mention that women also turn in some contemporary Mevlevi and Sufi circles.

Editor: hook corrected to match the ceremony and the teach: the turners enter in black cloaks, set them aside to show the white robes, and the reed flute's solo is no longer called the very first thing; screen line and the Masnavi link adjusted to match.
